newsitem.title: USA: Election finances probe favored by majority - poll.
newsitem.headline: Election finances probe favored by majority - poll.

text.p: A majority of Americans think planned congressional investigations of questionable fundraising by President Bill Clinton's election campaign are worthwhile, according to a CBS News poll released on Saturday.
The survey showed that Americans were paying more attention to reports about possibly illegal campaign contributions to the Democratic Party from foreign businessmen.
A total of 58 percent said they had heard or read "a lot" or "some" about the controversy, compared to 41 percent in October when the issue first was raised.
Congressional hearings were favoured by 53 percent of those interviewed, while 41 percent said they were unnecessary.
The poll was conducted among a nationwide sample of 1,001 adults by telephone on Dec. 4-5. It has a margin of error of plus or minus three percentage points.

Senate Republican leader Trent Lott said on Friday the Governmental Affairs Committee would proceed with an investigation of the Democrats' fundraising activities "immediately upon the swearing in of the 105th Congress on Jan. 7, 1977."

The inquiry will be headed by the committee's incoming chairman, Sen. Fred Thompson, R-Tennessee, who was the Republican counsel on the Senate Watergate Committee that investigated wrongdoing in the Nixon administration.
Other investigations into the affair that has embarrassed the White House are getting under way in the House of Representatives.
